summary: Language concepts and translation on one side, computer graphics algorithms on the other — a split unit where the graphics half is almost entirely formula-driven and therefore very scoreable.

topics.title: Language Design and Translation Issues
topics.summary: Paradigms, binding times, syntax specification and the stages a compiler runs through.

blocks.text:
A programming language is an interface between a way of thinking about computation and a machine that only shuffles bits. Everything in this topic follows from that tension: the language wants to be expressive, the machine wants to be simple, and the translator stands between them.

## Paradigms and models

A **paradigm** is a stance on what a program fundamentally *is*.

| Paradigm | A program is… | Languages |
|---|---|---|
| Imperative / procedural | a sequence of commands that mutate state | C, Pascal, FORTRAN |
| Object oriented | a set of objects exchanging messages | C++, Java, Smalltalk |
| Functional | the evaluation of mathematical functions, no side effects | Haskell, Lisp, ML |
| Logic / declarative | a set of facts and rules, with the answer inferred | Prolog |

The underlying **computational models** are the von Neumann model for imperative languages, lambda calculus for functional ones, and predicate logic with resolution for logic ones. Exam questions usually just want the language-to-paradigm pairing, but the model column is what makes the pairing non-arbitrary.

A **virtual computer** is the machine a language pretends to run on. C pretends you have a flat byte-addressable memory and a stack; Java pretends you have the JVM. The translator's job is to implement that pretend machine on the real one.

## Binding and binding time

**Binding** is fixing an attribute of a program entity to a specific value. **Binding time** is *when* that happens — and this single idea is asked almost every year.

| Binding time | What gets fixed | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Language design time | the meaning of `+`, the set of keywords | `if` is a keyword in C |
| Language implementation time | the size of `int`, the range of `float` | `int` is 4 bytes on this compiler |
| Compile time | the type of a variable, the structure of a record | `int x;` binds x's type |
| Link time | addresses of external functions | `printf` resolved from libc |
| Load time | absolute memory addresses of static variables | globals get real addresses |
| Run time | the value of a variable, the target of a virtual call | `x = 5;` or dynamic dispatch |

The general rule: **earlier binding means more efficiency, later binding means more flexibility**. A statically typed language binds types at compile time and can generate tight code; a dynamically typed one binds at run time and can do things a compiler could never check.

blocks.title: Ordering binding times
blocks.text: Whenever a question asks you to order binding times, order them by *how much of the program must exist yet*. Language design needs nothing; implementation needs a compiler; compile time needs your source; link time needs other objects; load time needs an OS; run time needs input. That ordering is always the answer.

## Syntax specification

Syntax is specified with a **context-free grammar**, usually written in BNF:

```
<expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>
<term> ::= <term> * <factor> | <factor>
<factor> ::= ( <expr> ) | id
```

**EBNF** adds convenience: `{ }` for zero-or-more, `[ ]` for optional, `( | )` for grouping. It expresses nothing BNF cannot — it is shorthand, not extra power.

The layering of the grammar above is deliberate. Because `<term>` sits below `<expr>`, multiplication binds tighter than addition; because the recursion is on the left, both operators associate left. Precedence and associativity are **encoded in the shape of the grammar**, not declared separately.

A grammar is **ambiguous** if some sentence has two distinct parse trees. The classic case is `if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2` — the dangling else. Real languages resolve it by rule (the `else` matches the nearest unmatched `if`) or by requiring an explicit terminator.

blocks.title: Worked example — why the grammar shape matters
blocks.text:
Parse `a + b * c` with the grammar above.

`<expr>` must split as `<expr> + <term>`. The left part derives `a`. The right part is a single `<term>`, which derives `<term> * <factor>` → `b * c`.

So the tree groups `b * c` first: the result is `a + (b * c)`. There is no derivation that produces `(a + b) * c`, because `<term>` cannot derive an expression containing an unparenthesised `+`. The precedence is structural.

Now flip the recursion to `<expr> ::= <term> + <expr>`. The grammar still accepts the same strings, but `a - b - c` would now group as `a - (b - c)` — right associative — and give the wrong arithmetic. Recursion side determines associativity: **left recursion gives left associativity.**

## Stages in translation

A compiler is conventionally six phases, the first three called the front end (analysis) and the last three the back end (synthesis).

| Phase | Input → Output | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| Lexical analysis | characters → tokens | illegal characters, malformed numbers |
| Syntax analysis | tokens → parse tree | missing semicolon, unbalanced brackets |
| Semantic analysis | parse tree → annotated tree | type mismatch, undeclared variable |
| Intermediate code generation | annotated tree → three-address code | — |
| Code optimisation | IR → better IR | — |
| Code generation | IR → target code | — |

The **symbol table** and **error handler** run alongside every phase rather than being phases themselves.

An **interpreter** skips code generation and executes the intermediate form directly: slower per operation, but no separate build step and easier to make portable. A **hybrid** system like Java compiles to bytecode ahead of time and interprets or JIT-compiles it at run time — early binding where it is cheap, late binding where it buys portability.

blocks.title: Which phase reports which error
blocks.text: `int x = "hello";` is **not** a syntax error — it parses perfectly. It is a *semantic* error, caught in semantic analysis by type checking. A missing semicolon is syntax. An undeclared identifier is semantic (the lexer happily produces an `id` token; nobody has checked it exists yet). Exam questions lean on exactly this distinction.

blocks.q: In which phase of compilation is the error in `float f; f = f + "abc";` detected?
blocks.exp: The string is a valid token and the assignment is a valid statement shape, so lexing and parsing both succeed. Only when types are checked does adding a string to a float become an error, and type checking happens in semantic analysis.

blocks.q: Binding the size of `int` to 32 bits happens at which time?
blocks.exp: The C standard deliberately leaves the width of `int` open, so it is not fixed at language design time. A particular compiler for a particular platform fixes it — that is language implementation time.

tricks.title: Paradigm from the question's verb
tricks.body: If a question describes a program as *stating relationships* it is logic; as *applying functions with no state* it is functional; as *sending messages between objects* it is OO; as *stepping through commands* it is imperative. Match the verb, not the language name.

tricks.title: EBNF adds no power
tricks.body: Any claim that EBNF describes languages BNF cannot is false. `{X}` is just `A ::= XA | ε`. Both describe exactly the context-free languages.

tricks.title: Left recursion ⇒ left associativity
tricks.body: You can read associativity straight off the production without drawing a tree. The recursive non-terminal's side is the side that groups first.

tricks.title: Six phases, two halves
tricks.body: Front end depends on the source language only; back end depends on the target machine only. That split is why one front end can serve many machines — and it is the answer to "why intermediate code at all?"

traps.title: Compiler vs interpreter speed
traps.body: Interpreters are slower at *execution*, but often faster at *development* because there is no compile-link cycle. A question asking which is "faster" without qualification usually means execution.

traps.title: Static vs dynamic binding is not static vs dynamic typing
traps.body: Binding time is about when an attribute is fixed; typing discipline is about whether types are checked at compile time. C is statically typed but uses dynamic binding for function pointers.

traps.title: Parse tree vs syntax tree
traps.body: A parse tree contains every grammar symbol including non-terminals used purely for precedence. An abstract syntax tree drops them. Questions about "the tree the parser produces" mean the parse tree.

topics.title: Elementary Data Types
topics.summary: Types as sets of values plus operations; l-values, type equivalence, coercion and array address arithmetic.

blocks.text:
A **data type** is a set of values together with the operations allowed on them. That definition does real work: it is why `int` and `float` are different types even when both hold the number 3, and why adding a pointer to a pointer is an error while adding an integer to a pointer is not.

An **object** in this sense (nothing to do with OOP) is a run-time container: it has a location, a lifetime, and a value.

## l-values and r-values

Every expression has an **r-value** — the value it denotes. Some expressions also have an **l-value** — a location that can be assigned to.

```c
x = y + 1;   /* x needs an l-value; y + 1 supplies only an r-value */
y + 1 = x;   /* error: left side has no location */
```

Array names are the classic trap: `a` has an r-value (the address of `a[0]`) but **no l-value** — you cannot write `a = b;` for arrays. A pointer `p` has both, which is why `p = b;` is fine.

## Scalar and composite types

**Scalar (primitive)** types hold one indivisible value: integers, reals, booleans, characters, enumerations and pointers. Enumerations are ordinal — their values have a defined successor — which is why they can index arrays and appear in `switch`.

**Composite (structured)** types are built from others:

| Type | Built by | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Array | Cartesian power of one type | n × sizeof(element) |
| Record / struct | Cartesian product of fields | sum of fields + padding |
| Union | disjoint sum — one field at a time | size of the largest field |
| Set | powerset of an ordinal type | implementation-defined bit vector |
| Pointer | reference to another object | word size |

The struct/union distinction is asked constantly: a struct holds **all** its members simultaneously, a union holds **exactly one** at a time and its members share storage.

blocks.title: Array address calculation
blocks.text:
For a **1-D** array `A[l … u]` with element size `w`:

$$\text{addr}(A[i]) = \text{base} + (i - l)\cdot w$$

For a **2-D** array `A[l_1..u_1][l_2..u_2]` with $n_2 = u_2 - l_2 + 1$ columns and $n_1$ rows:

**Row major** (C, Pascal — rows stored one after another):
$$\text{addr}(A[i][j]) = \text{base} + \big[(i-l_1)\cdot n_2 + (j-l_2)\big]\cdot w$$

**Column major** (FORTRAN — columns stored one after another):
$$\text{addr}(A[i][j]) = \text{base} + \big[(j-l_2)\cdot n_1 + (i-l_1)\big]\cdot w$$

blocks.title: Worked example — address in both orders
blocks.text:
`A[1..5][1..7]` is stored with base address 1000 and 2 bytes per element. Find the address of `A[3][5]`.

Here $l_1 = l_2 = 1$, $n_1 = 5$ rows, $n_2 = 7$ columns, $w = 2$.

**Row major:**
$1000 + [(3-1)\times 7 + (5-1)] \times 2 = 1000 + [14 + 4]\times 2 = 1000 + 36 = \mathbf{1036}$

**Column major:**
$1000 + [(5-1)\times 5 + (3-1)] \times 2 = 1000 + [20 + 2]\times 2 = 1000 + 44 = \mathbf{1044}$

The two differ because row major walks the *column* index fastest, column major walks the *row* index fastest. Notice which dimension count appears in each formula: row major multiplies by the number of **columns**, column major by the number of **rows**. Getting that backwards is the single most common error on these questions.

## Type equivalence

When are two types "the same"? Two rules exist and they disagree.

**Name equivalence:** two types are the same only if they have the same name (or one is declared directly from the other).

**Structural equivalence:** two types are the same if they are built identically, whatever they are called.

```c
typedef struct { int x; int y; } Point;
typedef struct { int x; int y; } Vector;
```

Under structural equivalence `Point` and `Vector` are interchangeable; under name equivalence they are not. C uses name equivalence for structs and unions (each `struct` declaration creates a new type) but structural equivalence for pointers and arrays. Pascal and Ada lean towards name equivalence; ML uses structural.

Name equivalence is stricter and catches more bugs — you cannot accidentally pass a `Metres` where `Feet` was wanted.

## Type checking and coercion

**Strong typing** means every type error is detected, at compile time or run time. **Weak typing** lets values be reinterpreted silently.

**Coercion** is an implicit conversion inserted by the compiler; **casting** is an explicit one you write. C's usual arithmetic conversions promote towards the wider type: `int + float` → both become `float`. Coercion weakens type checking — every coercion rule is a type error the compiler agreed not to report.

```c
int i = 5, j = 2;
float f = i / j;        /* f == 2.0, not 2.5 — integer division happens first */
float g = (float)i / j; /* g == 2.5 — the cast forces float division */
```

That first line is one of the most reliably examined single statements in the whole syllabus.

blocks.q: An array `X[1..10][1..15]` is stored in column-major order with base address 100 and each element occupying 4 bytes. What is the address of `X[5][8]`?
blocks.exp:
Column major with $n_1 = 10$ rows, $l_1 = l_2 = 1$, $w = 4$:

$100 + [(8-1)\times 10 + (5-1)]\times 4 = 100 + [70 + 4]\times 4 = 100 + 296 = 396$.

Note the multiplier is the number of **rows** (10), not columns — that is what makes it column major.

blocks.q: In C, which of these is NOT a valid l-value, given `int a[10], *p, x;`?
blocks.exp: An array name decays to a pointer *value* — it denotes the address of the first element but is not itself a modifiable location, so `a = ...` is illegal. `*p`, `a[3]` and `x` all name storage that can be assigned to.

tricks.title: Which dimension goes in the formula
tricks.body: Row major multiplies by the number of **columns**; column major multiplies by the number of **rows**. Mnemonic: the order you are NOT storing by is the one you multiply by.

tricks.title: Struct vs union size in one line
tricks.body: struct = sum of members (plus padding); union = max of members. If a question gives you both a struct and a union of the same members, the answers differ by exactly that.

tricks.title: Spot integer division instantly
tricks.body: In any expression, if both operands are integer types the operation is integer — regardless of what the result is assigned to. Scan for a float on at least one *operand*, never on the left-hand side.

tricks.title: Name equivalence is the stricter one
tricks.body: When asked which discipline rejects more programs, it is always name equivalence. Structural equivalence accepts everything name equivalence does, and more.

traps.title: Base address is the address of the first element
traps.body: Do not add one extra element width. Subtract the lower bound: for `A[1..n]` the offset of `A[1]` is zero, not `w`.

traps.title: Coercion is not casting
traps.body: Coercion is implicit and inserted by the compiler; a cast is written by you. A question about "implicit type conversion" means coercion.

traps.title: Enumerations are ordinal, pointers are not
traps.body: You can use an enum as an array index or a loop bound. Pointer arithmetic exists but pointers are not ordinal types in the sense meant by set and subrange constructors.

topics.title: Programming in C
topics.summary: Tokens, storage classes, pointers, structures, functions and the preprocessor — with the code-output puzzles the exam actually sets.

blocks.text:
C questions in this paper are rarely about writing programs. They are about predicting what a short fragment prints. That means the marks live in a handful of specific mechanisms — evaluation order, pointer arithmetic, storage duration, and macro expansion — rather than in general fluency.

## Tokens and storage classes

C's six token classes are keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and punctuators. There are 32 keywords in C89.

The four storage-class specifiers control three independent things: **storage duration**, **scope** and **linkage**.

| Specifier | Storage | Lifetime | Scope | Default value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | stack | block | block | garbage |
| `register` | CPU register if possible | block | block | garbage |
| `static` (local) | data segment | whole program | block | zero |
| `static` (global) | data segment | whole program | file only | zero |
| `extern` | data segment | whole program | global | zero |

The two meanings of `static` are the classic confusion: on a local variable it extends *lifetime*; on a global or a function it restricts *linkage* to the current file.

blocks.title: Worked example — static local

blocks.text:
## Operators, precedence and the sequence-point traps

The precedence facts worth memorising: unary operators bind tighter than binary; `*` and `/` above `+` and `-`; relational above equality; `&&` above `||`; assignment is right-associative and nearly lowest; the comma operator is lowest of all.

The traps are about **order of evaluation**, which C mostly does not specify:

```c
int i = 5;
printf("%d %d", i++, ++i);   /* undefined behaviour — order unspecified */
i = i++ + ++i;               /* undefined behaviour */
```

These are genuinely undefined, and different compilers print different things. Exam papers do sometimes ask them with a "expected" answer; when they do, the intended reading is usually right-to-left argument evaluation, but the defensible answer is that the behaviour is undefined.

Well-defined and heavily examined:

```c
int x = 5;
printf("%d", x++);   /* prints 5, x becomes 6 */
printf("%d", ++x);   /* x becomes 7, prints 7 */
int a = 0;
if (a++ && ++a) ;    /* && short-circuits: ++a never runs, a == 1 */
int b = 1;
if (b++ || ++b) ;    /* || short-circuits: ++b never runs, b == 2 */
```

## Arrays and pointers

An array name in an expression decays to a pointer to its first element. `a[i]` is *defined* as `*(a + i)`, which is why `a[i] == i[a]` compiles and works.

Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type: `p + 1` advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes, not one byte.

```c
int a[5] = {10,20,30,40,50};
int *p = a;
printf("%d", *(p+2));     /* 30 */
printf("%d", *p+2);       /* 12  — dereference first, then add */
printf("%ld", p+1 - p);   /* 1, not 4 — pointer difference is in elements */
```

The array/pointer distinction that matters:

| | `char s[] = "hi";` | `char *s = "hi";` |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | 3 bytes of writable array | pointer + string literal |
| `sizeof(s)` | 3 | 8 (pointer size) |
| `s[0] = 'H'` | legal | undefined — literals are read-only |
| `s = t` | illegal | legal |

Inside a function parameter list the two collapse: `void f(int a[])` and `void f(int *a)` declare exactly the same thing, which is why `sizeof` inside a function never gives you the caller's array length.

## Structures, unions and padding

```c
struct S { char c; int i; char d; };   /* sizeof typically 12, not 6 */
union  U { char c; int i; char d; };   /* sizeof 4 */
```

The struct is padded so each member sits at an address that is a multiple of its alignment: `c` at 0, three padding bytes, `i` at 4, `d` at 8, then three trailing padding bytes so an array of `S` stays aligned. The union's size is the largest member, rounded up to its alignment.

Structures are passed and assigned **by value** in C — copying a large struct copies every byte. Arrays are not, because the name decays.

## Functions and recursion

C passes everything **by value**. Passing a pointer does not make it call by reference; it makes it call by value where the value happens to be an address. That is why `swap(int a, int b)` cannot work and `swap(int *a, int *b)` can.

```c
int fact(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n-1); }
```

Each call pushes an activation record holding parameters, locals, the return address and the saved frame pointer. `fact(5)` reaches a stack depth of 5 before unwinding.

## File handling, command line arguments and the preprocessor

`fopen` returns a `FILE *` or `NULL`; modes are `r`, `w` (truncates), `a` (appends), plus `+` for update and `b` for binary. `fseek(fp, offset, origin)` with origin `SEEK_SET`, `SEEK_CUR` or `SEEK_END`; `ftell` reports the position; `rewind` resets it.

`int main(int argc, char *argv[])`: `argc` counts arguments **including the program name**, so running `./prog a b` gives `argc == 3`, `argv[0] == "./prog"`, and `argv[argc] == NULL`.

The preprocessor is pure text substitution before compilation. Its danger is that it does not respect expressions:

```c
#define SQR(x) x*x
SQR(2+3)      /* expands to 2+3*2+3 == 11, not 25 */

#define SQR2(x) ((x)*(x))
SQR2(2+3)     /* expands to ((2+3)*(2+3)) == 25 */

#define INC(x) ((x)+1)
INC(i++)      /* ((i++)+1) — fine; but a macro using x twice would increment twice */
```

Always parenthesise both the parameters and the whole macro body. Macros also have no type checking and no single evaluation guarantee, which is exactly why inline functions replaced them.

blocks.exp: `p` points at `a[2]`, which is 3. `p[-1]` is `*(p-1)` = `a[1]` = **2**. `*(a+4)` is `a[4]` = 5 and `*p` = 3, so the difference is **2**. Output: `2 2`. Negative subscripts are perfectly legal on a pointer that is not at the start of the array.

blocks.q: Given `#define CUBE(x) x*x*x`, what is the value of `CUBE(1+1)`?
blocks.exp: Text substitution gives the token sequence `1 + 1 * 1 + 1 * 1 + 1`. Applying precedence, the two multiplications are both $1\times1=1$, so the expression is $1+1+1+1 = \mathbf{4}$, not $2^3 = 8$. Writing the macro as `((x)*(x)*(x))` would give 8. This is the standard argument for parenthesising every macro parameter.

tricks.title: a[i] == *(a+i) == i[a]
tricks.body: Whenever a pointer question looks confusing, rewrite every subscript as pointer arithmetic. Half of these questions become trivial arithmetic once you do.

tricks.title: Short-circuit means the right operand may never run
tricks.body: In `&&`, if the left is 0 nothing on the right executes — including side effects. In `||`, if the left is non-zero the same. Track side effects only on the operands that actually evaluate.

tricks.title: struct = sum, union = max
tricks.body: With padding, round each member up to its own alignment and the total up to the largest alignment. If a question ignores padding it will use all-same-type members.

tricks.title: argc counts the program name
tricks.body: `./a.out x y z` gives argc = 4. Every question about command line arguments hinges on remembering the off-by-one.

tricks.title: static local initialises once
tricks.body: If a function with a static local is called n times, the initialiser ran once and the variable has accumulated n increments. Do not reset it mentally on each call.

traps.title: Pointer arithmetic is scaled
traps.body: `p + 1` moves `sizeof(*p)` bytes. If a question gives you addresses, multiply by the element size; if it gives you a pointer difference, the answer is in elements.

traps.title: `i = i++ + ++i` is undefined
traps.body: It is not a puzzle with a right answer — it is undefined behaviour. If an option says "undefined / compiler dependent", that is the correct choice.

traps.title: Arrays are not assignable, structs are
traps.body: `s1 = s2;` works for structs. `a1 = a2;` never works for arrays. This asymmetry is deliberately tested.

traps.title: `sizeof` an array parameter
traps.body: Inside `void f(int a[100])`, `sizeof(a)` is the size of a pointer, not 400. The array length is lost at the call boundary.

topics.title: Object Oriented Programming and C++
topics.summary: The four OOP pillars, then the C++ mechanisms the exam actually tests: construction order, overloading vs overriding, virtual functions and the diamond problem.

blocks.text:
## The four pillars

**Encapsulation** bundles data with the operations on it and hides the representation. **Abstraction** exposes what an object does while hiding how. **Inheritance** lets a class reuse and specialise another. **Polymorphism** lets one interface select among several implementations.

A **class** is a type; an **object** is an instance of it; **instantiation** is creating one. An **abstract class** cannot be instantiated because it has at least one pure virtual function.

Access specifiers control visibility:

| Specifier | Same class | Derived class | Outside |
|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | yes | no | no |
| `protected` | yes | yes | no |
| `public` | yes | yes | yes |

In C++ a `class` defaults to `private` members and private inheritance; a `struct` defaults to `public` for both. That single difference is the whole distinction between them.

## Constructors and destructors

A constructor has the class's name, no return type (not even `void`), and may be overloaded. A destructor has `~` plus the class name, takes no parameters, cannot be overloaded, and there is exactly one per class.

The ordering rules are examined relentlessly:

- **Construction:** base class first, then member objects in *declaration order*, then the derived constructor body.
- **Destruction:** exactly the reverse — derived body, then members in reverse declaration order, then base.

Member objects are constructed in the order they are **declared**, not the order they appear in the initialiser list. A constructor initialiser list that disagrees with declaration order is a classic compiler warning and a classic exam question.

blocks.title: Worked example — construction and destruction order

blocks.text:
## Overloading versus overriding

This is the most-asked distinction in the whole unit.

| | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Where | same scope | base and derived class |
| Signature | must **differ** | must be **identical** |
| Return type | may differ | must match (or be covariant) |
| Bound | compile time (static) | run time (dynamic), if `virtual` |
| Also called | ad-hoc / compile-time polymorphism | run-time polymorphism |

Overloading resolves on the argument types you wrote. Return type alone **cannot** distinguish overloads — `int f()` and `double f()` are a redeclaration error.

Operator overloading gives operators new meanings for user types. Four operators cannot be overloaded: `.`, `.*`, `::` and `?:` (and `sizeof`). Assignment, subscript, call and arrow must be non-static **member** functions.

## Virtual functions and dynamic dispatch

Declaring a member `virtual` means the call is resolved by the **dynamic** type of the object, not the static type of the pointer.

```cpp
class Base { public: virtual void f(){cout<<"B";} void g(){cout<<"b";} };
class Derv : public Base { public: void f(){cout<<"D";} void g(){cout<<"d";} };

Base *p = new Derv();
p->f();   // D — virtual, resolved at run time
p->g();   // b — non-virtual, resolved from the pointer's type
```

The mechanism is the **vtable**: each polymorphic class gets a table of function pointers, and each object gets a hidden `vptr` to its class's table. A virtual call is one extra indirection — which is why virtual functions cost a little and why `sizeof` a polymorphic class includes the vptr.

A **pure virtual** function `virtual void f() = 0;` makes the class abstract. You cannot instantiate it, but you can still have pointers and references to it — and that is exactly how polymorphism is used.

Destructors in any class meant to be inherited from should be virtual. `delete basePtr;` on a non-virtual destructor destroys only the base part.

## Inheritance types and the diamond problem

The access specifier on inheritance caps how inherited members appear:

| Base member | `public` inheritance | `protected` inheritance | `private` inheritance |
|---|---|---|---|
| public | public | protected | private |
| protected | protected | protected | private |
| private | inaccessible | inaccessible | inaccessible |

Private members of a base are never accessible in a derived class, whatever the inheritance mode.

The forms are single, multilevel (A→B→C), hierarchical (one base, many derived), multiple (one derived, many bases) and hybrid.

**Multiple inheritance** creates the **diamond problem**: if `B` and `C` both derive from `A`, and `D` derives from both, `D` contains two copies of `A` and any reference to an `A` member is ambiguous. The fix is **virtual inheritance**:

```cpp
class B : virtual public A { };
class C : virtual public A { };
class D : public B, public C { };   // exactly one A sub-object
```

With `virtual`, the most-derived class `D` is responsible for constructing the shared `A`.

## Templates, exceptions, streams

A **template** is a compile-time pattern; the compiler instantiates a separate concrete class or function for each type used. Templates give **parametric** polymorphism, distinct from the inheritance-based kind.

**Exceptions:** `throw` raises, `try` guards, `catch` handles. Stack unwinding destroys every automatic object between throw and catch, so destructors run. `catch(...)` catches everything and must come last. An uncaught exception calls `terminate()`.

**Streams:** `cin`/`cout`/`cerr`/`clog`, with `<<` and `>>` overloaded per type. File streams are `ifstream`, `ofstream`, `fstream`. Manipulators like `setw`, `setprecision` and `endl` format output; `endl` also flushes, `\n` does not.

blocks.q: Which statement is true of a C++ copy constructor?
opts: Its parameter must be passed by reference, otherwise the definition is infinitely recursive
It can be overloaded with a by-value version for efficiency
It is called when an object is assigned to an existing object
It cannot be declared for a class that has a destructor
blocks.exp: Passing the argument by value would itself require a copy, which would invoke the copy constructor again — the compiler rejects `T(T)` for exactly this reason. Assigning to an *already constructed* object calls `operator=`, not the copy constructor; and a class with a destructor managing resources is precisely the case that most needs a copy constructor.

blocks.q: For `class A{}; class B: virtual public A{}; class C: virtual public A{}; class D: public B, public C{};` how many sub-objects of type A does a D object contain?
blocks.exp: Virtual inheritance exists precisely to collapse the duplicate base. Without `virtual`, D would hold two A sub-objects and every access to an A member would be ambiguous; with it there is exactly **one**, constructed by the most-derived class D.

tricks.title: Construction order is always base → members → body
tricks.body: And destruction is the exact reverse. Write the constructor output forwards, then write it backwards in lower case, and you have the destructor output.

tricks.title: Virtual or not decides which function runs
tricks.body: For `Base *p = new Derived;` — if the function is virtual you get Derived's, otherwise you get Base's. That single check answers most polymorphism questions.

tricks.title: Members construct in declaration order
tricks.body: Not initialiser-list order. If a question lists them in a different order in the initialiser list, that is the trap.

tricks.title: Overload = different signature, same scope
tricks.body: If the two functions are in base and derived with the same signature, it is overriding. If they are in the same class with different parameters, it is overloading. Return type never counts.

tricks.title: Four operators cannot be overloaded
tricks.body: `.`  `.*`  `::`  `?:` — plus `sizeof`. Every other operator can be.

traps.title: Overriding needs an identical signature
traps.body: `void f(int)` in the base and `void f(double)` in the derived does not override — it *hides* the base version. Hiding is not overriding, and no virtual dispatch happens.

traps.title: Non-virtual destructor with delete-through-base
traps.body: `Base *p = new Derived; delete p;` with a non-virtual destructor is undefined behaviour and leaks the derived part. Any class with virtual functions should have a virtual destructor.

traps.title: Private members are never inherited-accessible
traps.body: Changing the inheritance mode to public does not expose the base's private members. Only protected and public members are reachable.

traps.title: struct vs class in C++
traps.body: They differ only in default access (public for struct, private for class). A struct in C++ can have constructors, methods and inheritance — unlike C.

topics.title: Web Programming: HTML, XML, Java, Servlets, Applets
topics.summary: Markup and its validity rules, client versus server scripting, and the lifecycle method sequences that get asked every year.

blocks.text: ## HTML and DHTML HTML is a markup language, not a programming language — it has no variables, no control flow and no computation. A document is a tree of elements, each written as a start tag, content and an end tag. Structure: `` containing `` (metadata, ``, `<link>`, `<style>`, `<script>`) and `<body>` (visible content). Useful facts that recur: `<a href>` makes a hyperlink, `<img src alt>` is an empty element, tables are `<table><tr><td>`, forms use `method="GET"` (data in the URL query string, limited length, idempotent, cacheable) or `method="POST"` (data in the request body, no length limit, not idempotent). HTML5 added `<canvas>`, `<video>`, `<audio>`, `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<article>` and `<section>`. **DHTML** is not a language at all. It is the combination of HTML for structure, CSS for presentation, the **DOM** for programmatic access, and JavaScript to tie them together so a page can change after it has loaded.

## XML, DTD and Schema

XML carries **data**, HTML displays it. XML has no predefined tags — you invent them — and it is strict where HTML is forgiving.

Two levels of correctness, and the distinction is examined constantly:

- **Well-formed**: obeys XML's syntax rules — exactly one root element, every tag closed, correct nesting, attribute values quoted, case-sensitive matching tags.
- **Valid**: well-formed *and* conforms to a DTD or XML Schema.

Every valid document is well-formed; the converse is false.

| | DTD | XML Schema (XSD) |
|---|---|---|
| Written in | its own syntax | XML itself |
| Data types | essentially none (all text) | rich built-in and derived types |
| Namespaces | not supported | supported |
| Cardinality | `?` `*` `+` only | `minOccurs` / `maxOccurs` with any integers |
| Extensible | no | yes |

Related technologies: **XSLT** transforms XML into other formats, **XPath** addresses parts of a document, **XQuery** queries it, and **DOM** (tree in memory, random access, memory hungry) versus **SAX** (event-driven, streaming, low memory, forward only) are the two parsing models.

## Scripting: client side versus server side

**Client side** scripts run in the browser: JavaScript and VBScript. They give instant feedback, reduce round trips, and can validate a form before it is submitted — but the user can read and modify them, so client-side validation is a convenience, never a security control.

**Server side** scripts run on the server: servlets and JSP, PHP, ASP.NET. They can reach the database, they are invisible to the user, and they are the only place security decisions can be made.

The standard exam framing: *validation must be repeated on the server even if the client already did it*, because the client cannot be trusted.

## Java essentials for this syllabus

Java is compiled to **bytecode**, which the **JVM** interprets or JIT-compiles — hence "write once, run anywhere". The JDK contains the JRE, which contains the JVM.

Points that recur:

- Java has **no** pointers, no `goto` in use, no operator overloading, no multiple inheritance of classes — but a class may `implement` many **interfaces**.
- `final` on a class prevents inheritance, on a method prevents overriding, on a variable makes it a constant.
- `static` members belong to the class, not an instance.
- Everything is passed **by value**; for objects the value passed is the reference, so the callee can mutate the object but cannot rebind the caller's variable.
- Memory is reclaimed by the **garbage collector**; `finalize()` is not a destructor and its timing is not guaranteed.
- An **abstract class** may hold state and concrete methods; an **interface** (classically) may not.

blocks.title: The two lifecycles — memorise these sequences
blocks.text:
**Applet** (runs in the browser, extends `java.applet.Applet`):

$$\texttt{init()} \to \texttt{start()} \to \texttt{paint()} \to \texttt{stop()} \to \texttt{destroy()}$$

`init()` runs **once** when the applet is loaded. `start()` runs after init and again every time the page is revisited. `stop()` runs when the page is left. `destroy()` runs once at unload. An applet has **no `main()`**.

**Servlet** (runs on the server, extends `HttpServlet`):

$$\texttt{init()} \to \texttt{service()} \to \texttt{destroy()}$$

`init()` runs **once**, when the servlet is first loaded. `service()` runs **once per request** and dispatches to `doGet()`, `doPost()`, `doPut()` and so on by HTTP method. `destroy()` runs once when the container unloads the servlet.

The crucial contrast: a servlet is instantiated **once** and its `service()` method is called on a **new thread per request** — so servlet instance variables are shared across users and are a concurrency hazard.

## Servlets in a little more detail

A servlet's request and response are `HttpServletRequest` and `HttpServletResponse`. Session tracking has four mechanisms: cookies, URL rewriting, hidden form fields, and the `HttpSession` API (which itself uses cookies or URL rewriting underneath).

**JSP** is servlets written inside-out: a page of HTML with Java embedded, which the container translates into a servlet source file, compiles, and then runs. Its own lifecycle is `jspInit()` → `_jspService()` → `jspDestroy()`, mapping straight onto the servlet lifecycle.

**Applets versus servlets** as a comparison table is a common question shape: applet on the client / servlet on the server; applet needs a browser JVM and a plugin / servlet needs a web container; applet has `init/start/paint/stop/destroy` / servlet has `init/service/destroy`; applets are effectively obsolete, servlets are not.

blocks.q: An XML document has correctly nested tags, quoted attribute values and a single root element, but no DTD is associated with it. The document is:
blocks.exp: Well-formedness is purely syntactic and this document satisfies it. Validity means conformance to a DTD or schema, and with no DTD there is nothing to conform to — so the document cannot be called valid. Validity always implies well-formedness, never the reverse.

blocks.q: In the applet lifecycle, which method is invoked every time the user returns to the page containing the applet?
blocks.exp: `init()` and `destroy()` each run exactly once, at load and unload. `start()` runs after `init()` and again on every revisit, paired with `stop()` on every departure. `paint()` runs whenever the display needs redrawing, which is related but not what "returning to the page" specifically triggers.

tricks.title: Applet: I-S-P-S-D
tricks.body: init, start, paint, stop, destroy. The two that run once are the two on the outside. Servlet keeps only the outer pair plus service: init, service, destroy.

tricks.title: Valid ⇒ well-formed, never the reverse
tricks.body: Any question offering both terms is testing this one-way implication. Absence of a DTD makes validity undefined, not true.

tricks.title: GET vs POST in one line
tricks.body: GET puts data in the URL (visible, length-limited, cacheable, idempotent); POST puts it in the body (hidden, unlimited, not cacheable). Anything about bookmarking or length is GET/POST.

tricks.title: One servlet instance, many threads
tricks.body: Whenever a question mentions servlet instance variables and concurrent users, the answer involves thread safety — because the container does not create a new servlet per request.

traps.title: DHTML is not a language
traps.body: It is HTML + CSS + DOM + scripting. Any option describing it as a markup or programming language is wrong.

traps.title: Java passes object references by value
traps.body: Reassigning the parameter inside a method does not affect the caller. Mutating the object it points to does. "Java is call by reference" is false.

traps.title: Applets have no main()
traps.body: Execution starts at `init()`, driven by the browser. A question offering `main()` as the applet entry point is offering a distractor.

traps.title: Client-side validation is not security
traps.body: It improves responsiveness only. Any question about where validation must happen for safety answers "server".

topics.title: Graphics Devices and Scan Conversion Algorithms
topics.summary: Display hardware, frame buffer sizing, and the incremental line, circle and ellipse algorithms with their decision parameters.

blocks.text:
## Display devices

In a **CRT**, an electron gun fires at a phosphor-coated screen; the phosphor glows briefly, so the image must be **refreshed**, typically 60–80 times a second. Below about 25 Hz the eye sees flicker.

Two scanning strategies:

| | Raster scan | Random (vector) scan |
|---|---|---|
| Beam path | every pixel, row by row | only along the lines to be drawn |
| Storage | frame buffer of intensity values | display list of drawing commands |
| Best at | realistic shaded scenes | line drawings, CAD |
| Resolution limit | pixel grid; lines show jaggies | very high, smooth lines |
| Cost | cheaper | dearer |

**Interlacing** draws odd-numbered scan lines on one pass and even on the next, halving the data rate needed for a flicker-free image — the trick television used for decades.

Colour CRTs use either the **beam penetration** method (two phosphor layers, limited colours, cheap, for random-scan) or the **shadow mask** method (RGB triads, full colour, for raster).

Other technologies worth naming: plasma panels, LCD (light-emitting versus light-modulating is the usual framing), LED and DVST — the direct view storage tube, which needs no refreshing at all because the image is stored on a grid inside the tube.

blocks.title: Frame buffer size
blocks.text:
$$\text{frame buffer bits} = \text{horizontal pixels} \times \text{vertical pixels} \times \text{bits per pixel}$$

with $\text{bits per pixel} = \lceil \log_2(\text{number of colours}) \rceil$.

For a 1024 × 768 display with 65 536 colours: $\log_2 65536 = 16$ bits per pixel, so $1024 \times 768 \times 16 = 12\,582\,912$ bits $= 1\,572\,864$ bytes $= \mathbf{1.5\text{ MB}}$.

Access rate for a refresh of $R$ Hz is frame buffer size × $R$ per second.

## Why incremental algorithms

The line $y = mx + c$ needs a multiplication and a rounding per pixel. Every algorithm below exists to replace that with additions on integers, because a display draws millions of pixels and floating point was once expensive.

## DDA — digital differential analyser

Compute $\Delta x = x_2-x_1$, $\Delta y = y_2-y_1$, and $\text{steps} = \max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)$. Then

$$x_{inc} = \Delta x/\text{steps}, \qquad y_{inc} = \Delta y/\text{steps}$$

and step from the start point adding the increments, rounding each coordinate to plot.

DDA is simple but uses **floating point** accumulation, so it is slower and accumulates rounding error over a long line.

blocks.title: Bresenham's line algorithm
blocks.text:
For a line in the first octant ($0 \le m \le 1$, $\Delta x > 0$), with $\Delta x = x_2-x_1$ and $\Delta y = y_2-y_1$:

Initial decision parameter:
$$p_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$$

At each step, plot $(x_k, y_k)$ then:

- if $p_k < 0$:  $x_{k+1} = x_k + 1$, $y_{k+1} = y_k$,  $p_{k+1} = p_k + 2\Delta y$
- if $p_k \ge 0$: $x_{k+1} = x_k + 1$, $y_{k+1} = y_k + 1$, $p_{k+1} = p_k + 2\Delta y - 2\Delta x$

Everything is **integer** — that is the whole advantage over DDA.

blocks.title: Midpoint circle and ellipse
blocks.text:
**Circle** of radius $r$ centred at the origin, drawing the second octant from $(0,r)$:

$$p_0 = 1 - r$$

- if $p_k < 0$: choose $(x_k+1,\ y_k)$ and $p_{k+1} = p_k + 2x_{k+1} + 1$
- if $p_k \ge 0$: choose $(x_k+1,\ y_k-1)$ and $p_{k+1} = p_k + 2x_{k+1} + 1 - 2y_{k+1}$

Only one octant is computed; the other seven come free by **8-way symmetry**: $(\pm x, \pm y)$ and $(\pm y, \pm x)$.

**Ellipse** with semi-axes $r_x, r_y$ — two regions, split where the slope reaches $-1$, i.e. where $2r_y^2 x \ge 2r_x^2 y$:

Region 1 (slope $> -1$, step in $x$): $\;p1_0 = r_y^2 - r_x^2 r_y + \tfrac{1}{4}r_x^2$

Region 2 (slope $< -1$, step in $y$): $\;p2_0 = r_y^2(x+\tfrac12)^2 + r_x^2(y-1)^2 - r_x^2r_y^2$

An ellipse has only **4-way symmetry**, not 8 — a favourite one-mark question.

## Polygon filling

**Scan-line polygon fill**: for each scan line, find every intersection with a polygon edge, sort the $x$ values, and fill between them in pairs. Two rules handle the awkward cases — a vertex where the two edges go in the *same* $y$ direction counts **once**, where they go in *opposite* directions it counts **twice**; horizontal edges are ignored. This is the method real renderers use because it touches each pixel once.

**Boundary fill**: start at an interior seed and recursively colour neighbours until a pixel of the *boundary colour* is met. Use it when the region has a single known boundary colour.

**Flood fill**: start at a seed and replace every connected pixel of the *old interior colour*. Use it when the region is one colour but the boundary is many.

Both come in **4-connected** (N,S,E,W) and **8-connected** (adding diagonals) forms. 8-connected fills leak through diagonal gaps that a 4-connected fill would respect — and conversely, a 4-connected fill cannot get through a diagonal opening that 8-connected can.

blocks.q: For Bresenham's line algorithm applied to a line from (0,0) to (8,5), what is the initial decision parameter?
blocks.exp: $\Delta x = 8$, $\Delta y = 5$, so $p_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x = 10 - 8 = \mathbf{2}$. The other options are $\Delta y$, $2\Delta y-2\Delta x$ and $2\Delta y$ respectively — the standard distractor set.

blocks.q: A raster display has a resolution of 1280 × 1024 and supports 256 colours. What is the minimum frame buffer size?
blocks.exp: 256 colours needs $\log_2 256 = 8$ bits = 1 byte per pixel. So the buffer is $1280 \times 1024 \times 1 = 1\,310\,720$ bytes $= 1.25$ MB (taking 1 MB = 1024 KB).

tricks.title: Bresenham initial parameter
tricks.body: $p_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$ for lines, $p_0 = 1-r$ for circles. These two constants answer a surprising number of one-mark questions with no tracing at all.

tricks.title: Circle 8-way, ellipse 4-way
tricks.body: A circle is symmetric about both axes and both diagonals; an ellipse only about the two axes. Any question comparing the symmetry of the two is asking exactly this.

tricks.title: Bits per pixel from the colour count
tricks.body: Take $\log_2$ of the number of colours and round up. 16 colours → 4 bits, 256 → 8, 64K → 16, 16M (true colour) → 24.

tricks.title: DDA vs Bresenham in one word
tricks.body: Floating point. DDA uses it, Bresenham does not — which is why Bresenham is faster and free of accumulated error.

traps.title: Bresenham always steps the major axis
traps.body: In the first octant $x$ increments on every iteration; only $y$ is conditional. If $|m| > 1$ the roles swap. Applying the first-octant formulas to a steep line gives the wrong pixels.

traps.title: Boundary fill vs flood fill
traps.body: Boundary fill stops at a specified *boundary* colour; flood fill replaces a specified *interior* colour. The question tells you which colour is specified — that names the algorithm.

traps.title: Refresh rate is not resolution
traps.body: Frame buffer size depends on resolution and colour depth only. Refresh rate multiplies the required *access rate*, not the buffer size.

topics.title: 2-D Transformations, Viewing and Clipping
topics.summary: Transformation matrices, homogeneous coordinates, composite transforms, window-to-viewport mapping and the clipping algorithms.

blocks.text:
## The basic transformations

In ordinary 2-D coordinates, scaling and rotation are matrix multiplications but translation is an addition — and that inconsistency is a real problem, because you cannot combine a mixture of multiplications and additions into a single matrix.

**Homogeneous coordinates** fix it. Represent the point $(x,y)$ as $(x,y,1)$ and use $3\times3$ matrices. Now translation is a multiplication too, and *any* sequence of transformations collapses into one matrix product.

$$T(t_x,t_y)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&t_x\\0&1&t_y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \quad S(s_x,s_y)=\begin{bmatrix}s_x&0&0\\0&s_y&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \quad R(\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&0\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

Reflections are scalings with negative factors: about the $x$-axis is $S(1,-1)$, about the $y$-axis is $S(-1,1)$, about the origin is $S(-1,-1)$, about the line $y=x$ swaps the coordinates.

Shear moves points parallel to an axis in proportion to the other coordinate:

$$Sh_x=\begin{bmatrix}1&sh_x&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \qquad Sh_y=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\sh_y&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.text:
Matrix multiplication does not commute, so $T \cdot R \ne R \cdot T$. Rotating then translating is not the same as translating then rotating.

Two cases *do* commute: two successive translations, two successive rotations about the same point, two successive scalings about the same origin, and — a favourite question — a uniform scaling with a rotation. A **non-uniform** scaling and a rotation do **not** commute.

blocks.title: Worked example — rotation about an arbitrary point
blocks.text:
Rotate the point $(4,3)$ by $90°$ anticlockwise about the pivot $(2,2)$.

The standard decomposition is three steps: translate the pivot to the origin, rotate, translate back.

$$M = T(2,2)\cdot R(90°)\cdot T(-2,-2)$$

Step 1 — translate by $(-2,-2)$: $(4,3) \to (2,1)$.

Step 2 — rotate $90°$: $(x,y) \to (-y, x)$, so $(2,1) \to (-1,2)$.

Step 3 — translate back by $(2,2)$: $(-1,2) \to (1,4)$.

The image is $\mathbf{(1,4)}$.

Check it: the pivot-to-point vector was $(2,1)$, length $\sqrt5$; the new vector is $(-1,2)$, also length $\sqrt5$, and rotated a quarter turn anticlockwise. Distances from the pivot are preserved, as any rotation must.

The same sandwich works for scaling about a fixed point and reflection about an arbitrary line — translate the special point to the origin, do the simple transform, translate back. Note that the matrices are written **right to left** in the order the point meets them.

blocks.title: Window-to-viewport transformation
blocks.text:
The **window** is the rectangle of world coordinates you want to see; the **viewport** is the rectangle of device coordinates you want to see it in.

Scaling factors:
$$s_x=\frac{xv_{max}-xv_{min}}{xw_{max}-xw_{min}} \qquad s_y=\frac{yv_{max}-yv_{min}}{yw_{max}-yw_{min}}$$

Mapping of a point:
$$xv = xv_{min} + (xw - xw_{min})\,s_x \qquad yv = yv_{min} + (yw - yw_{min})\,s_y$$

If $s_x \ne s_y$ the image is distorted — objects stretch. Keeping $s_x = s_y$ preserves the aspect ratio.

blocks.title: Worked example — window to viewport
blocks.text:
Window $(0,0)$ to $(10,10)$; viewport $(0,0)$ to $(200,100)$. Where does the world point $(6,4)$ land?

$s_x = (200-0)/(10-0) = 20$ and $s_y = (100-0)/(10-0) = 10$.

$xv = 0 + (6-0)\times 20 = 120$
$yv = 0 + (4-0)\times 10 = 40$

The device point is $\mathbf{(120,40)}$.

Because $s_x \ne s_y$ the picture is stretched twice as wide as it is tall — a circle in the window becomes an ellipse in the viewport. That observation is itself a common exam question.

## The 2-D viewing pipeline

World coordinates → **viewing coordinates** (apply the viewing transformation) → **normalised coordinates** (map the window to a unit square, so the rest is device independent) → **device coordinates** (map to the viewport on the actual screen).

Clipping is normally done in normalised coordinates, after the window transformation and before the device mapping.

blocks.title: Cohen–Sutherland region codes
blocks.text:
Each endpoint gets a 4-bit code relative to the clipping window. Using the Hearn and Baker ordering, bit 1 is the least significant:

| bit | set when |
|---|---|
| 1 (value 1) | point is **left** of the window, $x < xw_{min}$ |
| 2 (value 2) | point is **right** of the window, $x > xw_{max}$ |
| 3 (value 4) | point is **below** the window, $y < yw_{min}$ |
| 4 (value 8) | point is **above** the window, $y > yw_{max}$ |

The two decisions:

- **Trivially accept** if $\text{code}_1 \;|\; \text{code}_2 = 0000$ — both endpoints inside.
- **Trivially reject** if $\text{code}_1 \;\&\; \text{code}_2 \ne 0000$ — both endpoints share an outside region.
- Otherwise clip against one boundary at a time, recompute the code, and repeat.

blocks.title: Worked example — Cohen–Sutherland
blocks.text:
Window: $x$ from 0 to 10, $y$ from 0 to 10. Clip the line from $A(-2, 5)$ to $B(6, 14)$.

Code of $A$: $x = -2 < 0$ so the left bit is set; $y = 5$ is inside. Code $= 0001$.
Code of $B$: $x = 6$ is inside; $y = 14 > 10$ so the top bit is set. Code $= 1000$.

OR $= 1001 \ne 0$, so not trivially accepted. AND $= 0000$, so not trivially rejected. The line must be clipped.

Slope $m = (14-5)/(6-(-2)) = 9/8$.

Clip $A$ against the left edge $x = 0$: $y = 5 + \tfrac98(0-(-2)) = 5 + 2.25 = 7.25$. New $A = (0,\,7.25)$, code $0000$.

Clip $B$ against the top edge $y = 10$: $x = 6 + \tfrac{8}{9}(10-14) = 6 - 3.56 = 2.44$. New $B = (2.44,\,10)$, code $0000$.

Both codes are now zero, so the visible segment runs from $\mathbf{(0,\,7.25)}$ to $\mathbf{(2.44,\,10)}$.

## The other clippers

**Liang–Barsky** is parametric. Write the line as $x = x_1 + u\Delta x$, $y = y_1 + u\Delta y$ with $u \in [0,1]$, and solve four inequalities $u\,p_k \le q_k$. It is more efficient than Cohen–Sutherland because it computes the intersection parameters directly instead of clipping repeatedly against edges, and it does only one division per candidate.

**Sutherland–Hodgman** clips a **polygon** against each window edge in turn, feeding the output of one stage into the next. For each edge pair it outputs: both inside → the second vertex; inside to outside → the intersection; outside to inside → the intersection then the second vertex; both outside → nothing. Its known weakness is that clipping a concave polygon can leave spurious connecting edges; **Weiler–Atherton** fixes that and handles concave polygons correctly.

blocks.q: A window has corners (0,0) and (100,50); the viewport has corners (0,0) and (400,400). What are the scaling factors $s_x$ and $s_y$?
blocks.exp: $s_x = (400-0)/(100-0) = 4$ and $s_y = (400-0)/(50-0) = 8$. Because they differ, the image is stretched vertically — a square in the window becomes a rectangle twice as tall as it is wide.

blocks.q: Two endpoints of a line have Cohen–Sutherland region codes 0100 and 0110. The line is:
opts: partially visible and must be clipped
blocks.exp: The bitwise AND is $0100 \wedge 0110 = 0100 \ne 0000$, meaning both endpoints lie below the window (that bit is set in both). A line with both endpoints on the same outside side of a boundary cannot cross the window, so it is trivially rejected without any intersection arithmetic.

tricks.title: Any transform about a fixed point is a sandwich
tricks.body: $T(p)\cdot M\cdot T(-p)$. Rotation about a point, scaling about a point, reflection about an arbitrary line — all the same three-step pattern. Never derive it from scratch.

tricks.title: Rotation by 90°, 180°, 270° without trigonometry
tricks.body: $90°$: $(x,y)\to(-y,x)$. $180°$: $(x,y)\to(-x,-y)$. $270°$: $(x,y)\to(y,-x)$. All anticlockwise. This turns a matrix question into one line.

tricks.title: Trivial accept/reject in one bit operation
tricks.body: OR the codes — zero means accept. AND the codes — non-zero means reject. Anything else needs clipping. You rarely need to compute an intersection at all.

tricks.title: Aspect ratio distortion
tricks.body: If a question asks whether a shape is distorted by a window-to-viewport map, just compare $s_x$ and $s_y$. Equal means faithful, unequal means stretched.

traps.title: Matrix order is right to left
traps.body: In $M = T\cdot R\cdot S$ applied as $M\cdot P$, the point is scaled first, then rotated, then translated. Reading the product left to right gives the reverse of the actual sequence.

traps.title: Reflection about y = x is not a rotation
traps.body: It swaps coordinates: $(x,y)\to(y,x)$. Its determinant is $-1$, so it reverses orientation — rotations never do.

traps.title: Sutherland–Hodgman and concave polygons
traps.body: It clips them, but can produce connecting edges between separated pieces. If a question asks which algorithm handles concave polygons correctly, the answer is Weiler–Atherton.

topics.title: 3-D Representation, Transformations and Viewing
topics.summary: Surfaces and splines, Bezier and B-spline properties, illumination and shading models, and projection.

blocks.text:
## Representing 3-D objects

**Polygon surfaces** are the workhorse: an object is a mesh of planar facets stored as a vertex table, an edge table and a surface-facet table. Every renderer reduces to triangles eventually because a triangle is guaranteed planar and convex.

A plane is $Ax+By+Cz+D=0$, and $(A,B,C)$ is its **normal vector** — the quantity every lighting calculation needs.

**Quadric surfaces** are described by second-degree equations: the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=r^2$, the ellipsoid $(x/r_x)^2+(y/r_y)^2+(z/r_z)^2=1$, plus tori, cones and cylinders. They are compact and exact, but harder to render than polygons.

3-D transformations extend the 2-D ones to $4\times4$ homogeneous matrices. Rotation now needs an **axis**: $R_z$ looks exactly like the 2-D rotation with $z$ untouched, and $R_x$, $R_y$ are the cyclic permutations of it.

## Splines

A **spline** is a piecewise polynomial curve. It is specified by **control points**, and the three continuity conditions at a join are $C^0$ (positions meet), $C^1$ (tangents match), $C^2$ (curvature matches).

A curve **interpolates** its control points if it passes through them and **approximates** them if it merely follows their shape. Bezier and B-spline curves approximate; only the endpoints are touched.

blocks.title: Bezier curves
blocks.text:
A Bezier curve of degree $n$ with $n+1$ control points $p_k$:

$$P(u)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} p_k\,B_{k,n}(u), \qquad u\in[0,1]$$

with the **Bernstein basis** polynomials

$$B_{k,n}(u)=\binom{n}{k}u^k(1-u)^{n-k}$$

Properties, all examinable:

- Degree is $n$ where $n+1$ is the number of control points. **Four control points give a cubic.**
- The curve passes through $p_0$ and $p_n$ only.
- It is tangent to $p_1-p_0$ at the start and to $p_n-p_{n-1}$ at the end.
- It lies inside the **convex hull** of its control points.
- The basis functions sum to 1 for every $u$ (partition of unity).
- Moving one control point changes the **whole** curve — there is no local control.

## B-splines versus Bezier

The B-spline exists to fix Bezier's two weaknesses.

| | Bezier | B-spline |
|---|---|---|
| Degree | fixed by the number of control points | chosen independently ($d$) |
| Local control | no — one point affects everything | **yes** — a point affects only $d$ spans |
| Continuity at joins | must be arranged by hand | $C^{d-2}$ automatically |
| Convex hull | whole curve in one hull | each span in its own smaller hull, so a tighter bound |
| Special case | — | a B-spline with $d = n+1$ *is* a Bezier curve |

For a B-spline with $n+1$ control points and order $d$ the knot vector has $n+d+1$ values. **NURBS** — non-uniform rational B-splines — add weights per control point and can represent conic sections exactly, which plain B-splines cannot.

Surfaces are the tensor product of two curve formulations: a bicubic Bezier patch has a $4\times4$ grid of 16 control points.

blocks.title: Illumination models
blocks.text:
**Ambient:** a constant background term, $I = k_a I_a$. It has no direction and no position.

**Diffuse (Lambert's cosine law):** matte surfaces scatter light equally in all directions, so brightness depends only on the angle between the surface normal $N$ and the light direction $L$:

$$I_{diff}=k_d\,I_l\,(N\cdot L)=k_d I_l\cos\theta$$

It is **independent of the viewer's position** — that is the defining property.

**Specular (Phong):** shiny highlights, depending on the angle between the reflection vector $R$ and the viewer $V$:

$$I_{spec}=k_s\,I_l\,(R\cdot V)^{n_s}$$

The exponent $n_s$ is the shininess: large $n_s$ gives a small tight highlight, small $n_s$ a broad dull one. Unlike diffuse, this term **does** depend on where the viewer is.

Total: $I = k_aI_a + \sum_{lights}\big[k_dI_l(N\cdot L) + k_sI_l(R\cdot V)^{n_s}\big]$

## Polygon rendering methods

| Method | What is interpolated | Cost | Highlights |
|---|---|---|---|
| Constant (flat) | nothing — one intensity per facet | cheapest | facets clearly visible, Mach bands |
| Gouraud | **intensity** across the polygon | moderate | misses a highlight that falls inside a facet |
| Phong | the **normal vector**, then lighting per pixel | dearest | renders highlights correctly |

The examinable distinction in one line: **Gouraud interpolates intensities, Phong interpolates normals.** Phong is slower because the lighting equation is evaluated at every pixel rather than at every vertex, and that is precisely why it gets specular highlights right.

## The 3-D viewing pipeline and projection

Modelling coordinates → world coordinates → viewing coordinates → projection coordinates → normalised coordinates → device coordinates.

**Parallel projection**: projectors are parallel; the view volume is a rectangular box. It preserves relative proportions, so it is used for engineering drawings, but it does not look realistic.

- *Orthographic* — projectors perpendicular to the view plane. Front, top and side elevations; the axonometric variant is the isometric view.
- *Oblique* — projectors at an angle. Cavalier keeps the depth axis at full scale; cabinet halves it.

**Perspective projection**: projectors converge at a centre of projection. The view volume is a **frustum**. Distant objects shrink — *perspective foreshortening* — which looks realistic but destroys measurable proportions. The number of **vanishing points** (one, two or three) is set by how many principal axes the view plane cuts.

$$\text{perspective: } x_p=\frac{x}{1+z/d}, \quad y_p=\frac{y}{1+z/d}$$

3-D clipping works against the six planes of the view volume; the Cohen–Sutherland idea extends to a **6-bit** region code.

blocks.q: A Bezier curve is defined by 5 control points. What is its degree, and how many control points does it pass through?
blocks.exp: With $n+1 = 5$ control points the degree is $n = 4$. A Bezier curve interpolates only its first and last control points — the intermediate three pull the curve towards them but are not touched. So: degree 4, passes through 2.

blocks.q: Which shading model interpolates surface normals across a polygon rather than intensities?
blocks.exp: Gouraud computes intensity at each vertex and interpolates the intensity; Phong interpolates the **normal vector** and evaluates the full lighting equation per pixel. That extra work is what lets Phong render a specular highlight that falls in the middle of a polygon, which Gouraud simply misses.

tricks.title: n+1 control points ⇒ degree n
tricks.body: Four control points give a cubic Bezier, the most common case. The question almost always gives the count and wants the degree, or the reverse.

tricks.title: Diffuse ignores the viewer, specular does not
tricks.body: If a question asks which term is independent of viewing position, the answer is diffuse every time. The $N\cdot L$ formula contains no $V$.

tricks.title: Gouraud = intensity, Phong = normal
tricks.body: Four words that answer every shading comparison question, including which one is slower and which one handles highlights.

tricks.title: Parallel preserves proportion, perspective preserves realism
tricks.body: Whenever a question asks which projection is used for engineering drawings, it is parallel/orthographic; for realistic images it is perspective.

tricks.title: B-spline wins on local control
tricks.body: Every Bezier-versus-B-spline question comes down to one of: independent degree, local control, or automatic continuity. All three favour the B-spline.

traps.title: Bezier curves do not interpolate interior points
traps.body: The curve only touches $p_0$ and $p_n$. Options claiming it passes through all control points describe an interpolating spline, not a Bezier.

traps.title: Convex hull is a bound, not the shape
traps.body: The curve lies *within* the hull of its control points; it does not follow the hull. B-splines give a tighter bound because each span uses only its own local points.

traps.title: Perspective foreshortening breaks measurement
traps.body: Perspective views look right but you cannot read dimensions off them. That is exactly why parallel projection survives in CAD.

traps.title: Phong shading vs the Phong illumination model
traps.body: They are different things. The Phong *illumination model* is the specular term; Phong *shading* is normal-vector interpolation. A question may use either sense.
